conbody.p: Is reverting back to the old way of doing things the best method to leveling the playing field? Without the CASE Act, the process of litigating copyright law is extensive, leaving both parties waiting for months on end for a decision from a federal court and draining the pockets of the defendant in the meantime. Due to the rise of the internet, the ease of committing copyright violations has increased tenfold. Because of the requirement that infringement claims be heard federally, copyright litigation has the potential to clog court dockets all for a relatively petty act. Additionally, should the CASE Act be repealed, the maximum amount awarded in statutory damages as it currently stands federally, does not reflect the cost of the crime of illegal downloading. The statutory damages awarded in such cases are often arbitrary, inconsistent, and excessive. One of the most striking examples, as legal scholar Matthew Sag points out in his article, is Capitol Records v. Thomas-Rasset, [where the] jury awarded statutory damages of more than $1.92 million against a defendant who had illegally downloaded about $54 worth of music…a ratio of more than 35,000 to 1. It is because of this cost and waiting time that the defendant has a fighting chance, however, as the process goes on, the stakes increase. As time goes on the defendant faces larger financial ruin than they might face under the CASE Act and the punishment increasingly does not fit the crime.
